full_text_en:
Hyosung (HK) Ltd. v. China Shipping Agency Co., Ltd., Fangchenggang Branch et al. — dispute over bill of lading infringement (appeal)

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2002) Min Si Zhong Zi No. 27

Appellant (Plaintiff at First Instance): Hyosung (HK) Ltd. (formerly known as Hyosung Products Hong Kong Ltd.), HYOSUNG (HK) LTD. Domicile: Room 2504, 25th Floor, 9 Queen's Road Central, Central, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.

Legal Representative: Park Chan-sun, General Manager of the Company.

Authorized Representative: Cao Nanjiang, Lawyer of Kangda Law Firm.

Authorized Representative: Gao Zicheng, Lawyer of Kangda Law Firm.

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance): China Shipping Agency Co., Ltd., Fangchenggang Branch. Domicile: 2nd Floor, Foreign Trade Building, Fangchenggang City, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region.

Legal Representative: Ou Enqiang, Manager of the Branch.

Authorized Representative: Xie Wei, Lawyer of Far East Law Firm.

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance): China Sinotrans Guangxi Company. Domicile: No. 137 Qixing Road, Nanning City, Guangxi.

Legal Representative: Ou Enqiang, Manager of the Company.

Authorized Representative: Xie Wei, Lawyer of Far East Law Firm.

Authorized Representative: Yun Yi, Lawyer of Beijing Tianmao Law Firm.

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance): Agricultural Bank of China, Wuzhou Branch. Domicile: No. 62 Bubu Road, Wuzhou City, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region.

Responsible Person: Hua Weiqiang, President of the Branch.

Authorized Representative: Zou Weining, Lawyer of Junhe Law Firm.

Authorized Representative: Li Zengli, Lawyer of Junhe Law Firm.

The appellant Hyosung (HK) Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Hyosung) appealed to this Court against the civil judgment (2001) Gui Jing Chu Zi No. 18 rendered by the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region High People's Court in the dispute over bill of lading infringement with the respondents China Shipping Agency Co., Ltd., Fangchenggang Branch (hereinafter referred to as Fangcheng PSD), China Sinotrans Guangxi Company (hereinafter referred to as Guangxi Sinotrans), and Agricultural Bank of China, Wuzhou Branch (hereinafter referred to as Wuzhou ABC). This Court formed a collegial panel according to law and held a public hearing of this case. The authorized representatives of the appellant Hyosung, Cao Nanjiang and Gao Zicheng; the authorized representatives of the respondents Fangcheng PSD and Guangxi Sinotrans, Xie Wei; the authorized representative of Guangxi Sinotrans, Yun Yi; and the representative litigant of the respondent Wuzhou ABC, Wu Baohong, and its authorized representatives Zou Weining and Li Zengli, appeared before the court. The case is now concluded.

The findings at first instance were as follows: On February 25, 1997, Hyosung entered into a "Urea Purchase and Sale Contract" with Hong Kong Zhide International Trade Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Zhide), stipulating that Hyosung would supply Zhide with 28,000 tons of urea at a unit price of US$200/ton. Pursuant to this contract, on March 10, 1997, Zhide entered into a "Sales Contract" with the Sixth Branch of Guangxi Fangchenggang Import and Export Company (hereinafter referred to as the Sixth Branch), stipulating that Zhide would supply the Sixth Branch with 28,000 tons of urea at a unit price of US$210.8/ton, price term CIFFO Fangchenggang, China, with a total amount of US$5,902,400. The payment term required the buyer to issue an irrevocable usance letter of credit for 180 days before March 19, 1997. On April 3, 1997, Zhide chartered the vessel "Xilaier" to transport the 28,000 tons of urea supplied by Hyosung to Fangchenggang. The "Xilaier" issued a full set of three original bills of lading held by Hyosung. After the goods arrived at port, the Sixth Branch entrusted Fangcheng PSD with customs declaration for the cargo, and Fangcheng PSD declared to customs and completed customs clearance procedures for 9,000 tons of urea. On April 17, the Sixth Branch and Wuzhou ABC respectively issued letters of guarantee to Fangcheng PSD, guaranteeing to submit the original bill of lading as soon as possible and requesting Fangcheng PSD to release the goods for delivery. From April 18 to July 19, Fangcheng PSD delivered a total of 9,000 tons of goods to the Sixth Branch. Since the Sixth Branch was unable to obtain an import license and the bank did not allow the opening of a letter of credit, in order to protect the interests of both parties, on July 21, Hyosung, the Sixth Branch, and Zhide entered into an "Agreement" (hereinafter referred to as the Tripartite Agreement), stipulating: Party A (the Sixth Branch) must guarantee Party B's (Hyosung) cost, with the purchase price calculated at Party B's cost price of US$194/ton; Party A shall open letters of credit for other goods and discount them to Zhide for onward payment to Party B as payment for the urea, with specified arrangements for the timing, bank, and amount of the letters of credit, and all payments must be fully settled by discount no later than August 15; Party B shall actively cooperate with Party A in handling customs declaration and clearance, and shall not miss the July-August agricultural urea sales season; if Party A fails to perform as above, all losses shall be borne by Party C (Zhide). After the contract was signed, due to the lack of an import license, Fangcheng PSD was unable to complete customs clearance. On September 11, 1997, Fangchenggang Customs, on the grounds that the goods had exceeded the time limit for customs declaration without declaration, seized and sold 19,245.8 tons of urea carried by the "Xilaier". After deducting taxes and other expenses, on June 12, 1998, Customs notified Fangcheng PSD to notify the cargo owner to process the refund. On April 22, 1998, Hyosung delivered one original bill of lading to Zhide for transfer to the Sixth Branch, so that the Sixth Branch could handle the refund procedures with Customs for 19,000 tons of urea. In the same year, Hyosung filed a lawsuit against the Sixth Branch with the Fangchenggang Intermediate People's Court, alleging: it was the holder of the bill of lading for the goods on the "Xilaier"; Fangcheng PSD was the shipping and cargo agent for the vessel; on June 6, 1997, Fangcheng PSD split the bill of lading and took delivery of 9,000 tons of urea; on September 11, 1997, Customs sold the remaining goods and required the shipping agent to notify the cargo owner, but Fangcheng PSD failed to notify in time, resulting in no notification; therefore, it requested the court to confirm that it was the holder of the full set of original bills of lading for the "Xilaier", and that the remaining proceeds of US$16,702,311.55 from the Customs sale of the 19,245.8 tons of urea carried by the "Xilaier" belonged to it. After mediation by the court, the parties voluntarily reached an agreement: the Sixth Branch confirmed that Hyosung was the owner of the full set of original bills of lading for the "Xilaier", and that the remaining proceeds of 16,702,311.55 yuan from the 19,245.8 tons of urea under the bill of lading belonged to Hyosung. The mediation document (［1998］Fang Zhong Fa Jing Chu Zi No. 80) has been executed and is effective. Hyosung, in order to recover the payment for 9,000 tons of urea, previously filed a lawsuit with the Nanning Intermediate People's Court on June 1, 1999, based on the "Sales Contract" which contained an arbitration clause, but was dismissed by the Nanning Intermediate People's Court. During the period from 1998 to 2001, Hyosung annually applied to the Hong Kong courts and Singapore courts for arrest orders against vessels to preserve the statute of limitations for this case. On March 28, 2001, Hyosung filed a lawsuit with the court of first instance based on the original bill of lading for the goods on the "Xilaier", requesting the court to confirm that the three defendants had delivered goods without the original bill of lading, thereby infringing on Hyosung's ownership of the goods under the bill of lading.

The court of first instance held: As to whether the statute of limitations had expired in this case, the evidence submitted by Hyosung showed that Hyosung had been applying to the Hong Kong and Singapore courts to arrest vessels of the carrier of the goods under the bill of lading within the limitation period. Therefore, Hyosung's action against the parties who are jointly and severally liable with the carrier did not exceed the statute of limitations. As to whether Hyosung was the sole owner of the bill of lading for the goods in this case and had the right to bring an infringement action based on the legal effect of the bill of lading, this case involves two legal relationships: first, the legal relationship of compensation for damage caused by delivery of goods without the original bill of lading and taking delivery of goods; second, the legal relationship of international sale of goods. At the time the goods arrived at port, Hyosung legally held the original bill of lading and was the owner of the goods under the bill of lading. Fangcheng PSD, as the shipping agent and tally clerk, delivered the goods to the Sixth Branch based on a letter of guarantee rather than the original bill of lading, which violated international trade practices. Wuzhou ABC, by issuing a letter of guarantee to provide security for the Sixth Branch's taking delivery of goods without the original bill of lading, also violated international trade practices. However, Hyosung did not assert its rights against Fangcheng PSD and Wuzhou ABC based on the property right of the bill of lading. Instead, knowing that the import license could not be obtained due to policy reasons, the bank did not allow the opening of a letter of credit, and Fangcheng PSD had released the goods after splitting the bill of lading, Hyosung, in the capacity of the cargo owner under the international sale contract, renegotiated with the Sixth Branch on price, payment terms, and breach of contract, and entered into the Tripartite Agreement. In particular, the payment method was changed from payment for the urea by letter of credit to discounting letters of credit for other goods to Zhide, indicating that the bill of lading held by Hyosung no longer had the effect of a document of title, but was merely evidence of the contract of carriage and delivery of goods. In addition, Hyosung also sued the Sixth Branch, requesting the Sixth Branch to recover the payment for the over 19,000 tons of goods sold by Customs. Its conduct demonstrated that Hyosung recognized the Sixth Branch as the person entitled to the goods under the bill of lading, and that Hyosung held a claim against the Sixth Branch, and could legally request the Sixth Branch to pay the price. Therefore, the issuance of the letter of guarantee by Wuzhou ABC to Fangcheng PSD, and the release of goods by Fangcheng PSD in accordance with the instructions of the cargo owner, the Sixth Branch, did not constitute infringement against Hyosung. Hyosung's claim, based on a bill of lading without the effect of a document of title, that the three defendants had infringed its rights and sought compensation for the payment of 9,000 tons of urea under the bill of lading, lacked merit and was not supported. The dispute over payment between Hyosung and the Sixth Branch should be resolved separately. In accordance with Article 72, Paragraph 2 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, which states that "property obtained by contract or other lawful means, the ownership of property shall be transferred at the time of delivery", after discussion by the judicial committee, it was decided: to dismiss Hyosung's claims. The case acceptance fee of 125,860 yuan shall be borne by Hyosung.

Hyosung, dissatisfied with the above judgment, appealed to this Court, requesting that the judgment of first instance be reversed and that Fangcheng PSD be ordered to compensate it for the payment of 9,000 tons of urea in the amount of US$1,897,200, equivalent to RMB 15,746,760, plus interest of RMB 6,224,379.2, totaling RMB 21,971,139.2. Guangxi Sinotrans and Wuzhou ABC shall bear joint and several liability for compensation. The reasons were: 1. The court of first instance did not allow the key evidence for establishing the case, i.e., the Tripartite Agreement, to be cross-examined, and thus it could not serve as the basis for the decision; the court of first instance used a single copy of the Tripartite Agreement as the basis for finding facts, and the formal requirements of the evidence were seriously deficient; the procedure of the first instance violated the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China and the Supreme People's Court's Several Provisions on Evidence in Civil Proceedings, resulting in incorrect factual findings. 2. The Tripartite Agreement could not negate the effect of the bill of lading as a document of title. The Tripartite Agreement was false evidence, and there was no other evidence to prove that Hyosung had abandoned its property right in the goods; Fangcheng PSD and Wuzhou ABC, in violation of international trade practices, delivered goods without the bill of lading to the Sixth Branch first, and this act constituted an infringement of Hyosung's property rights. Hyosung could, within the statutory limitation period, choose at its discretion the time and manner to assert its rights against Fangcheng PSD and Wuzhou ABC, unless Hyosung expressly waived this right; the loss of the property-right attribute of a bill of lading requires a formal act. Only after the buyer pays and redeems the bill of lading, and the carrier delivers against the bill of lading, does the property-right attribute cease. The goods in question have not yet been delivered against the bill of lading, and the Sixth Branch never obtained and could not have obtained ownership of the goods in question; assuming the Sixth Branch obtained ownership of the goods under the relevant bill of lading pursuant to the Tripartite Agreement, in the civil mediation document (1998) Fang Zhong Fa Jing Chu Zi No. 80, the Sixth Branch confirmed Hyosung as the owner of the 19,245.8 tons of urea under the bill of lading. This indicates that Hyosung never lost ownership of the goods under the bill of lading, and when the 9,000 tons of goods were disposed of without authority by the three respondents, the bill of lading had not lost its effect as a document of title. 3. Hyosung's lawsuit against the Sixth Branch to recover the proceeds of the goods sold by Customs was clear evidence of Hyosung's assertion of its property right, not a basis for the loss of the property right in the bill of lading.

Fangcheng PSD argued in its response: 1. The finding of the first instance that the copy of the Tripartite Agreement had evidentiary effect was in accordance with the law; this evidence was produced in court during the first instance trial and cross-examined by Hyosung. Although the Tripartite Agreement was a copy, Hyosung submitted it to the court when filing its lawsuit with the Nanning Intermediate People's Court, and also made statements about the Tripartite Agreement in its complaint; thus, the authenticity of the Tripartite Agreement and its use as the basis for the decision are beyond doubt. 2. The statute of limitations for this case has expired, and Hyosung's claims should not be supported. According to the Maritime Code, "the limitation period for claims for compensation for loss of or damage to goods in carriage of goods by sea is one year, counting from the date on which the carrier delivered or should have delivered the goods." The limitation period for claims against the carrier's agent for compensation for loss or damage in carriage of goods by sea should also be one year. In this case, although Hyosung sued the carrier and applied to arrest the carrier's vessel carrying the goods in question in the Singapore High Court in March 1998, the Singapore High Court dismissed Hyosung's claim by order on December 7, 2000. According to Article 267 of the Maritime Code, the limitation period for Hyosung's lawsuit against the carrier and its agent was not interrupted by the March 1998 lawsuit and vessel arrest. Even if Hyosung filed a lawsuit against Fangcheng PSD et al. with the Nanning Intermediate People's Court in June 1999, that lawsuit was dismissed by the Nanning Intermediate People's Court, and the June 1999 lawsuit also did not interrupt the limitation period under the law. Furthermore, the view of the first instance that Hyosung had been applying to the Hong Kong and Singapore courts to arrest the vessel of the carrier of the goods under the bill of lading during the limitation period, and therefore Hyosung's lawsuit against the parties who are jointly and severally liable with the carrier (i.e., the shipping agent as the carrier's agent) did not exceed the statute of limitations, lacks legal basis. 3. The finding of the first instance that the bill of lading held by Hyosung no longer had the effect of a document of title was based on fact and law. 4. Fangcheng PSD agreed to allow the Sixth Branch to take delivery of goods without the bill of lading based on the company letter of guarantee issued by the Sixth Branch and the bank letter of guarantee issued by Wuzhou ABC, for which Wuzhou ABC should bear liability as guarantor. 5. The entity sued by Hyosung as "China Shipping Agency Company Guangxi Fangchenggang Branch" was the former name of Fangcheng PSD, which was later approved by the State Administration for Industry and Commerce to be changed to "Guangxi Fangchenggang Shipping Agency Company." However, in practice, Fangcheng PSD has been using the name "China Shipping Agency Company Guangxi Fangchenggang Branch" to conduct business. The shipping agency acts disputed in this case performed by China Shipping Agency Company Fangchenggang Branch were actually the acts of Fangcheng PSD. It requested that Hyosung's claims be dismissed.

Guangxi Sinotrans's response, in addition to agreeing with Fangcheng PSD's responses on points 1, 2, and 4, also presented the following: 1. According to international practice, after the carrier discharges the goods at the port of destination, the goods are placed under the management of the carrier's agent at the port of destination, and the carrier's shipping agent delivers the goods to the holder of the bill of lading. In this case, Fangcheng PSD, as the carrier's agent at the port of destination, was the only entity with the authority to decide the delivery of the goods. The entity that delivered the goods without the bill of lading in this case was Fangcheng PSD, not Guangxi Sinotrans. Guangxi Sinotrans was not the carrier's shipping agent and had no authority to decide the delivery of the goods; therefore, it could not possibly be the party responsible for the delivery of goods without the bill of lading as alleged by Hyosung. It requested that Hyosung's claims be dismissed. 2. Guangxi Sinotrans was the customs declaration agent for the Sixth Branch and did not directly engage in any infringing conduct. 3. Hyosung did not point out any specific facts of Guangxi Sinotrans delivering goods without the bill of lading, but only generally asserted that Guangxi Sinotrans and Fangcheng PSD jointly delivered goods without the bill of lading. It requested that the judgment of first instance be upheld.

Wuzhou ABC argued in its response: 1. The Tripartite Agreement was provided by Hyosung itself, is credible, and can be used as evidence in this case. 2. Through the Tripartite Agreement, Hyosung ratified the Sixth Branch's unlawful possession of the goods and confirmed the existence of a creditor-debtor relationship with the Sixth Branch. Hyosung had previously filed a lawsuit based on the Tripartite Agreement, and the civil mediation document (1998) Fang Zhong Fa Jing Chu Zi No. 80 cannot affect the effect of the Tripartite Agreement in discharging Wuzhou ABC's guarantee liability. 3. There is no causal relationship between Wuzhou ABC's issuance of the letter of guarantee and Hyosung's loss. Wuzhou ABC further argued that the judgment of first instance found the facts clearly and applied the law correctly, and requested this Court to dismiss Hyosung's appeal in accordance with the law and in line with the spirit of this Court's Reply (2000) Jiao Ta Zi No. 1.

The bill of lading, the letter of guarantee issued by Wuzhou ABC, the delivery receipt, and the arrest order of the Singapore High Court, which were cross-examined during the trial of first instance, are hereby admitted by this Court. The authenticity of the civil mediation document (1998) Fang Zhong Fa Jing Chu Zi No. 80 of the Fangchenggang Intermediate People's Court and the authenticity of Hyosung's complaint to the Nanning Intermediate People's Court are confirmed. Other evidence found by the first instance, including the purchase and sale contract between Hyosung and Zhide, the sales contract between Zhide and the Sixth Branch, and customs documents, which were not objected to by all parties, are also confirmed by this Court.

During the trial before this Court, Hyosung submitted two new pieces of evidence: 1. An agreement dated June 16, 1997, between the Sixth Branch and Guangxi Arts & Crafts Import and Export Company, Wuzhou Branch (hereinafter referred to as Guangxi Arts & Crafts), concerning the transfer of 20,000 tons of urea. 2. A certificate issued by China Sinotrans Guangxi Fangchenggang Company on July 24, 1997, regarding the storage, customs declaration, and taking delivery of 28,245.8 tons of urea imported by Guangxi Arts & Crafts, to prove that Guangxi Arts & Crafts transferred the imported urea to the Sixth Branch, and that Guangxi Arts & Crafts entrusted Guangxi Sinotrans with customs declaration and the taking delivery of 9,000 tons of urea. Fangcheng PSD and Wuzhou ABC, during cross-examination, argued that these two materials were not originals and could not be verified. This Court holds that, according to the relevant provisions of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, documentary evidence should be provided in original form. Materials that are not originals and cannot be verified may not be used as evidence to establish facts. Therefore, the two pieces of evidence provided by Hyosung cannot be used as evidence to establish facts in this case.

Fangcheng PSD submitted notarized copies of three receipts of Guangxi Arts & Crafts and a notarization of the Tripartite Agreement issued by the Nanning Regional Notary Office, to prove that the Tripartite Agreement indeed existed. The notarization is an original, and its authenticity is confirmed by this Court.

Fangcheng PSD also submitted the complaint filed by the carrier of the goods in question, Xilaier Shipping Company, with the Beihai Maritime Court against Fangcheng PSD, Wuzhou ABC, and Guangxi Arts & Crafts for damages resulting from the arrest of its vessel due to the delivery of goods without the bill of lading, as well as the notice of appearance, summons from the Beihai Maritime Court, and the order of the Singapore High Court dated December 7, 2000, dismissing Hyosung's claim. Hyosung, during cross-examination, argued that Fangcheng PSD should produce the originals; that this evidence could not prove that the statute of limitations had expired in this case. This Court holds that, with respect to the order of the Singapore court, since there is no other evidence to corroborate it and the opposing party does not recognize it, it cannot be used as evidence.

After the court hearing, Fangchenggang Ocean Shipping Agency and Guangxi Foreign Transportation submitted to this court evidentiary materials, including the arrest order, order of release of the vessel, and the court order dismissing Hyosung's application for arrest of the vessel and the lawsuit, from the High Court of Singapore, as verified by the Beihai Maritime Court. Upon cross-examination by Hyosung, it contended that since these exhibits were all photocopies and the translation agency did not meet the relevant requirements, they should not be accepted. Wuzhou Agricultural Bank also refused to accept the evidence on the ground that it was not original. This court holds that although these evidentiary materials are all photocopies, for those materials verified to be consistent with the originals by the Beihai Maritime Court, this court affirms their authenticity. The other materials, not meeting the requirements of the relevant legal provisions, are not accepted by this court.

Wuzhou Agricultural Bank did not provide new evidence.

Regarding the validity of the tripartite agreement as evidence, the court of first instance did not conduct cross-examination during the trial, but only verified it after the trial. However, this evidentiary material was copied from the relevant case files of the Nanning Intermediate People's Court, which affixed a verification stamp on the copy. Furthermore, in the complaint filed by Hyosung with that court, the tripartite agreement and its specific contents were explicitly mentioned. The claim by Hyosung during the trial of this court denying the existence of the tripartite agreement contradicts its own claim in the separate lawsuit. The notarial certificate issued by Fangchenggang Ocean Shipping Agency during the trial of this court also confirms the existence of the tripartite agreement. These pieces of evidence can corroborate the actual existence of the tripartite agreement, and this court affirms it.

Additionally, during the trial of the first instance, the representatives of Fangchenggang Ocean Shipping Agency and Guangxi Foreign Transportation admitted in their defense that the specific entity that took delivery of the goods was Guangxi Arts and Crafts. During the trial of this court, Fangchenggang Ocean Shipping Agency also admitted that the delivery order was issued to the Sixth Branch, that the actual taking of delivery was jointly carried out by the Sixth Branch and Guangxi Arts and Crafts, that customs declaration was made under the name of another company, and that the Sixth Branch made payments to Guangxi Arts and Crafts. Based on the delivery order provided by Fangchenggang Ocean Shipping Agency (i.e., the small bill of exchange that should be exchanged for the original bill of lading), this court finds that the person taking delivery should be the Sixth Branch.

This court finds: Guangxi Foreign Transportation was the customs broker entrusted by the Sixth Branch for the goods after they arrived at the port. On September 11, 1997, the Fangchenggang Customs extracted and sold 19,245.8 tons of urea carried by the vessel "Xilaier" on the ground that the goods had exceeded the time limit for customs declaration without being declared. After deducting taxes and other fees, on June 12, 1998, the Customs notified Guangxi Foreign Transportation, requesting it to notify the relevant consignees to go through the refund procedures. However, Guangxi Foreign Transportation was required to notify the consignees to submit import documents and quota certificates for the goods to the Customs. If they failed to do so, the goods would be confiscated and the proceeds turned over to the state treasury in accordance with relevant regulations. The other facts found by the court of first instance are basically clear.

This court holds that this case is a dispute over tort involving a bill of lading with Hong Kong elements. The place where the tort occurred, i.e., the place where the goods were delivered without presentation of the original bill of lading, is Fangchenggang, Guangxi. The laws of the People's Republic of China shall apply as the lex causae of this case. This case mainly involves issues such as the validity of the bill of lading on which Hyosung based its lawsuit and whether the statute of limitations had expired.

Pursuant to Article 71 of the Maritime Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the "Maritime Law"), a bill of lading is a document used to prove the contract of carriage of goods by sea and that the goods have been received by the carrier or loaded on board, and a document by which the carrier undertakes to deliver the goods against surrender thereof. A clause in the bill of lading stating that the goods are to be delivered to the named consignee, or to the order of the named person, or to the bearer of the bill of lading, constitutes an undertaking by the carrier to deliver the goods accordingly. In this case, the bill of lading on which Hyosung relied in bringing the lawsuit and which was issued by the carrier is a blank order bill of lading, which had been endorsed by the shipper. Therefore, at the port of destination, the carrier should deliver the goods to the person holding the bill of lading. Hyosung, as the legal holder of the original bill of lading, has rights over the goods under the bill of lading that should be protected by law. Fangchenggang Ocean Shipping Agency, as the shipping agent, released part of the goods without seeing the original bill of lading, which violated the legal requirement that goods must be released against presentation of the bill of lading. Guangxi Foreign Transportation, as the customs broker for the goods after they arrived at the port, handled the customs declaration for its principal without the principal submitting the original bill of lading, which violated the relevant regulations. Wuzhou Agricultural Bank issued a letter of guarantee for the release of goods against a guarantee, which violated international trade practices.

However, the goods in question arrived at Fangchenggang Port on April 3, 1997. On April 18, June 6, and July 19, the Sixth Branch went through the procedures for taking delivery of the goods with Fangchenggang Ocean Shipping Agency. Three months after the goods arrived at the port, i.e., on July 21, Hyosung, Zhide Company, and the Sixth Branch entered into a tripartite agreement, making arrangements for the payment of the purchase price of the goods in question, thereby changing the payment method under the original sales contract. The true intent of all three parties was expressed, and the tripartite agreement aimed to facilitate the actual performance of the sales contract. The act of entering into the tripartite agreement indicated that Hyosung acknowledged the Sixth Branch as the actual buyer of the goods in question and recognized the Sixth Branch's status as the actual consignee. It can be determined that, after the goods arrived at the port but before the signing of the tripartite agreement, Hyosung had already confirmed the Sixth Branch's act of taking delivery of the goods. Because the Sixth Branch only had an import license for 9,000 tons of goods, the remaining 19,245.8 tons of goods were sold by the Customs due to the Sixth Branch's inability to provide legal import formalities. Hyosung did not demand payment of the purchase price or compensation for corresponding losses from the Sixth Branch, which had actually taken delivery of the goods. Instead, in the lawsuit filed by Hyosung against the Sixth Branch before the Fangchenggang Intermediate People's Court, Hyosung claimed that it was the holder of the full set of bills of lading and applied to the court for confirmation of its ownership of the balance of RMB 16,702,311.55 for the 19,245.8 tons of goods and the corresponding interest, but did not assert ownership of the 9,000 tons of goods that had already been taken delivery of by the Sixth Branch.

Pursuant to Article 21 of the Customs Law of the People's Republic of China (1987) (hereinafter referred to as the "Customs Law"), which was in force at the time the dispute arose, if the consignee of imported goods fails to declare to the Customs within three months from the date of declaration of entry of the means of transport, the imported goods shall be taken over and sold by the Customs. After deducting expenses for transportation, loading and unloading, storage, and taxes, if there is any surplus, it shall be returned to the consignee upon application within one year from the date of sale of the goods; if no application is made within the time limit, the surplus shall be turned over to the state treasury. Furthermore, according to Article 10 of the Implementing Regulations of the Customs Administrative Penalties of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the "Implementing Regulations"), which were approved by the State Council, where goods are imported or exported without a license in violation of state regulations on import and export management, the goods shall be confiscated or ordered to be returned; if a license is subsequently obtained upon approval by the licensing authority, a fine of not more than the value of the goods shall be imposed. Hyosung is a Hong Kong company, and it was unable to obtain an import license for the goods in question and could not retrieve the surplus. If the Sixth Branch had not taken delivery of the 9,000 tons of goods, those 9,000 tons of goods would have been sold by the Customs together with the other goods in accordance with the Customs Law and relevant regulations, and Hyosung would also have been unable to claim the surplus. Hyosung cannot assert any rights over the goods in question unless it returned the goods within the time limit prescribed by law. The document "Fangguanhan [1998] No. 2" from Fangchenggang Customs to Guangxi Foreign Transportation also confirms this point. This further demonstrates the reason for the emergence of the tripartite agreement, i.e., Hyosung gave up the right to return the goods, recognized the Sixth Branch's status as consignee, and only sought to ensure that it received payment. Therefore, although Hyosung holds the bill of lading, it can no longer assert its rights over the goods under the bill of lading against the relevant parties based on the bill of lading.

Article 257 of the Maritime Law provides that the statute of limitations for claims for compensation under a contract of carriage of goods by sea is one year, counting from the date on which the carrier delivered or should have delivered the goods. However, in this case, Hyosung did not sue the carrier, but rather sued the carrier's agent, Fangchenggang Ocean Shipping Agency, which delivered the goods at the port of destination, the customs broker Guangxi Foreign Transportation, and the guarantor for release of goods, Wuzhou Agricultural Bank, for delivering the goods without the original bill of lading. Fangchenggang Ocean Shipping Agency argued that the statute of limitations for this case should be determined as one year under the Maritime Law, but it did not prove that the delivery of goods without the bill of lading was within the scope of the carrier's authorization; therefore, its request cannot be upheld. The statute of limitations for Hyosung's claim against Wuzhou Agricultural Bank, as the guarantor for release of goods, and Guangxi Foreign Transportation, as the customs broker, also cannot be determined under the Maritime Law. The statute of limitations for this case should be determined in accordance with the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the "General Principles"). According to Articles 135 and 137 of the General Principles, the statute of limitations for applying to a people's court for protection of civil rights is two years, counting from the time when the right holder knew or should have known that the right was infringed. In this case, the goods arrived at the port on April 3, 1997, and the latest time was July 21, when the tripartite agreement was signed. Hyosung should have known that part of the goods had been taken delivery of by the Sixth Branch. Therefore, the statute of limitations for this case should run from July 21, 1997, to July 21, 1999. On June 1, 1999, Hyosung and Zhide Company filed a lawsuit with the Nanning Intermediate People's Court against Fangchenggang Ocean Shipping Agency, Wuzhou Agricultural Bank, Guangxi Foreign Transportation, Fangchenggang Import and Export Trade Company, and others, requesting the court to order the defendants to compensate for losses in the amount of the purchase price of the 9,000 tons of goods under the bill of lading caused by breach of contract or tort. According to Article 140 of the General Principles, the statute of limitations is interrupted by the filing of a lawsuit, by a party's making of a claim, or by a party's agreement to perform an obligation. Therefore, the statute of limitations in this case was interrupted by Hyosung's filing of the lawsuit with the Nanning Intermediate People's Court. The statute of limitations for Hyosung to assert its rights has not exceeded the time limit prescribed by law.

In summary, this court holds that the judgment of the court of first instance was inaccurate in finding that the Customs notified Fangchenggang Ocean Shipping Agency to go through the refund procedures and in finding that the Sixth Branch entrusted Fangchenggang Ocean Shipping Agency with customs declaration. The failure to determine the status of Guangxi Foreign Transportation as the customs broker constitutes a finding of unclear facts in part. The judgment of the court of first instance failed to determine the basis for and the duration of the statute of limitations in this case, and its finding that Hyosung had been applying to the Hong Kong and Singapore courts for the arrest of the vessel of the carrier of the goods under the bill of lading within the statute of limitations, and therefore Hyosung's lawsuit against parties jointly and severally liable with the carrier did not exceed the statute of limitations, lacked a legal basis. However, the finding of the court of first instance that the bill of lading held by Hyosung does not have the effect of a document of title is correct, and Hyosung's claims should not be protected by law. The result of the judgment of the court of first instance is not improper and should be upheld.

Pursuant to Article 71 of the Maritime Law of the People's Republic of China and Articles 135, 137, and 140 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, the judgment is as follows:

Appeal rejected, and the original judgment affirmed.

The court costs of the first instance shall be borne as determined in the judgment of the first instance. The court costs of the second instance, RMB 125,860, shall be borne by the Appellant, Hyosung Hong Kong Co., Ltd.

This judgment is final.
